opening.headline: The problem of an agent's output deviating from policy is addressed using guardrails—code placed both before and after execution.
body: What should we do if a customer service agent causes expensive model inference by requesting a solution walkthrough, or inadvertently reveals another customer's personal information in their response? Simply instructing the system prompt to say "don't do it" is insufficient to prevent such actions. Instructions only express what the model is expected to follow; they do not serve as enforceable constraints.

Guardrails are checks executed in code, before and after tool calls, that validate user inputs and agent outputs. In this lesson, we examine the points at which guardrails intervene, their execution mechanisms, and the balance between over-constraining and under-constraining. We also provide case studies on deploying guardrails in customer service agents, distinguishing between issues that can be resolved with guardrails and those that require additional mechanisms.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the roles of input guardrails and output guardrails
The point at which guardrails are applied among input, tool, and output can be distinguished and deployed within the agent.

screens.title: An agent's output may violate the policy.
screens.lead: Read about two possible incidents that could actually occur in a customer service agent role. The diagram shows where these incidents take place.

visual.alt: A diagram illustrating two cognitive points along the flow where user input passes through an agent to generate a response.
labels: ① Expensive models are invoked in response to customer requests for homework solutions.
② Mixing of other customers' personal information in the response

paragraphs: There is a customer service agent responsible for handling refund inquiries and shipping updates. This agent uses an expensive model and order lookup tools. One day, two incidents occurred.

First, a customer requested help solving a math homework problem, and the agent responded using an expensive model. Second, personal information from another customer was inadvertently mixed into a response. The first is a problem related to cost and scope, while the second is a problem related to unsafe behavior.

Agents can violate policies for various reasons, including ambiguous instructions, model hallucinations, adversarial user escape and prompt injection, and indirect injections through tools. The risks manifest as harmful content that violates policies, statements inconsistent with brand guidelines, or the leakage of personal information—unsafe behaviors.
Telling a model not to do something is insufficient. Checks must be placed in both the front and back of execution through code. This is guardrails.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are the two approaches above—blocking on the input side or blocking on the output side—better? You will be able to answer this question with the reasons by the end of this class.

screens.outro: Let's first consider the order between input validation and output validation.

screens.title: View option: Should input validation or output validation come first?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What would we lose if we block the model before it processes dangerous requests?
items.answer: You can save costs, time, and side effects caused by tools by performing quick and inexpensive input validation before invoking a model. If you can filter out malicious inputs before a costly model starts, misuse will not result in financial loss. Therefore, input validation is performed prior to processing.

items.prompt: Can sensitive information generated by the model be caught by input validation?
items.answer: It cannot be retrieved. The response is a result generated by the model, therefore it does not exist during the input phase. Similarly, if personal information from other customers is mixed into the tool's output. Thus, separate output validation is required before being provided to the user.

items.prompt: What happens if an audit prevents the normal request from proceeding?
items.answer: Normal customers will be unable to use the service. An error that classifies a legitimate request as a violation is called a false positive. The more strictly the criteria are set, the safer it may appear, but false positives increase accordingly. Therefore, when setting criteria, a balance between false positives and false negatives must be considered.

screens.outro: Let's compare the thought process against the flow where guardrails actually intervene.

steps.title: Two types of guardrails
steps.body: Input guardrails perform validation on the user's initial input, while output guardrails validate the agent's final output. Guardrails can be applied to the functions and tools used by the agent. These three guardrails handle different points in the execution process.

steps.title: Step 1: Receive input
steps.body: Guardrails receive inputs similar to those passed to an agent. The validation function can either directly call an external classifier or execute a separate small agent. By quickly and cheaply validating with a lightweight model, you can filter out attacks before resorting to more expensive models, thus saving time and costs.

steps.title: Step 2: Create the inspection results
steps.body: The inspection function returns a result. The result contains information used in the decision-making process, as well as a tripwire (fail-safe switch) value indicating whether to halt. For example, if the function determines that the request is for a math homework assignment, the tripwire is set to active.

steps.title: Step 3: Verify the tripwire.
steps.body: If tripwire is triggered, an exception is raised and execution is halted. The application catches this exception and provides appropriate guidance to the user. The output guardrail also operates in the same three-stage process, and after verifying the final output, raises an exception if tripwire is triggered.

steps.title: Know the execution location.
steps.body: Input guards are executed only by the first agent in the chain, while output guards are executed only by the final agent that produces the output. Agents and tools in the middle of a workflow with extensive delegation fall outside the scope of this check. Tool guards are executed before input validation and after output generation whenever a function tool is invoked, so tool guards are separately placed adjacent to tools that may have side effects.

steps.title: The same structure in other implementations
steps.body: Google ADK also proposes the same approach: tool-level guardrails that embed policies within the tool, callbacks for validation before and after calls, and using lightweight, fast models as separate safety mechanisms. While the implementation tools may differ, the structural aspect of code-level verification before and after execution remains consistent.

screens.outro: Now, let's read the input guardrail in code and verify the difference between parallel execution and blocking execution.

screens.title: Input guardrail code reading: Parallel execution and blocking execution
screens.lead: The following is Python code for an input guardrail that prevents mathematical homework requests. Check the right-hand explanation for the meaning of each line and the symptoms that appear when values are inconsistent.

notes.note: The agent for testing and its output format. It receives the evaluation result as a boolean named is_math_homework and a reason string. The output format must be fixed so that the below function can reliably extract the tripwire value. By using a faster and cheaper model instead of an expensive one, cost can be saved.

If run_in_parallel is False, it means sequential execution. The guardrail starts first, and the agent begins only after the guardrail has completed. Therefore, when tripwire is enabled, the agent will not execute, preventing token consumption and tool side effects. The default value is True (parallel execution), in which case both the guardrail and the agent start simultaneously, minimizing delay. However, if tripwire is activated at that point, the agent may have already consumed tokens and executed tools.

This is a validation function. It executes the validator agent with the same inputs as received by the agent and returns the decision as a GuardrailFunctionOutput. If tripwire_triggered becomes True, an exception is raised and execution is terminated. Incorrectly inverting this value would block legitimate requests or allow violating requests to pass through.

This section attaches guardrails to agents. Each guardrail is attached to its respective agent, and input guardrails are executed only by the first agent in the chain. When calling the agent, the caller must catch the InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered exception and provide guidance to the user. If the exception is not caught, the user will only see an error.

screens.outro: The output guardrail will examine how this option differs, together with the threshold.

screens.title: False positives and misses, and threshold values
screens.lead: Move the slider to adjust the inspection criteria from loose to strict, and you can verify what passes and what is blocked based on the criteria.

visual.alt: A concept diagram illustrating the relationship where looser inspection criteria lead to increased mistakes, and stricter criteria lead to increased false alarms.

stops.body: It only filters violations when the threshold is set to HIGH and there is high confidence in the violation. Normal requests are unlikely to be blocked, resulting in low false positives. Instead, ambiguous violations are allowed through. This type of error—allowing violations—is called a false negative. As illustrated in the Model Armor documentation, when hate content is set to HIGH, it only detects cases reported with high confidence.

We filter out intermediate levels of confidence. This is a choice that balances between false alarms and missed detections. The appropriate threshold varies depending on the nature of the service. Services used by children may adopt a stricter threshold, while tools used by experts may adopt a more lenient one.

LOW_AND_ABOVE filters out even low confidence cases. Regardless of the confidence level (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), any violation is treated as a breach. While false positives may decrease, the misclassification of normal requests as violations increases, potentially blocking legitimate customers. It cannot be definitively stated that the stricter the policy, the safer it is.

Model Armor is a Google Cloud service that checks prompts before sending them to an LLM and verifies responses before delivering them to users. It detects and filters harmful, harassing, risky, and explicit content, as well as prompt injection, jailbreaking, and sensitive information exposure. If violations are detected, it blocks or obscures the content and returns details explaining which filter was applied. When integrated with an agent gateway, it consistently applies the same policies to all prompts and responses passing through the gateway. It logs inspection results, enables observation, and supports policy tuning regardless of the method used.

steps.title: Verify the target
steps.body: Customer service agent handling refund inquiries and shipping updates. Uses expensive models and order lookup tools. The initial concerns on the first screen were two: the expensive model handling out-of-scope requests, and response content containing mixed information from other customers.

steps.title: Step 1: Input guardrail
steps.body: Checks low-cost models for out-of-scope requests (such as homework solutions) and injection attempts. Since the goal is to avoid using expensive models, it blocks execution. The agent only starts after guardrails have completed, so if a request is blocked, the expensive model will not consume any tokens.

steps.title: Step 2: Tool Guard Rail
steps.body: Input and output guards are executed only at the first and last agents, so side effects of the order lookup tool are isolated separately beside the tool. Lookups are permitted only within the caller's account scope, and sensitive fields are excluded from responses. This reduces the pathway through which other customers' information could reach the response.

steps.title: Step 3: Output Guardrail
steps.body: Before finalizing the response for the user, we check the final output for any expressions that violate privacy or policies of other customers, and if such expressions are found, we replace the response with an alternative message. Output guards are executed after the agent completes its task, so there are no parallel options. Denied final outputs are not saved in the session, but the already completed tool call history is preserved.

steps.title: Step 4: Adjust the threshold value
steps.body: It is not sufficient to rely solely on batch processing. To establish appropriate criteria, one must simultaneously monitor the rate at which legitimate inquiries are blocked and the rate at which violations are erroneously approved. For this purpose, all inspection results are recorded. Without such records, there is no basis for adjusting or lifting the criteria.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: Once the initial question is answered, it is better to block input-side processing rather than output-side processing, because costs are avoided when filtering occurs before processing. Personal information leakage must be prevented on the output side as well, since responses are results generated by the model and are not visible at the input stage. To fully secure all three points, defense mechanisms must also be implemented on the tool side.

screens.outro: After completing the batch, let's determine what problem cannot be resolved solely by the guardrail.

screens.title: Problems solvable with guardrails and problems requiring different devices
screens.lead: The following table summarizes which device to use first depending on the nature of the problem. Read row by row and connect which device was needed in the earlier example.

data.caption: Nature of the issue and appropriate control mechanisms
rows: Automatically verifiable tests. Input violations, output violations, validation of tool arguments and results
Block out-of-scope requests, hide personal information in responses, validate tool call arguments
Judgments can be wrong, leading to misidentification and mistakes. Automated systems cannot replace human judgment in decisions that require it.
An action that may have adverse effects and requires approval from a person or policy before execution
Order cancellation, editing, shell commands, sensitive MCP operations, email transmission to external recipients
If approval requests are too frequent, people will press them without judgment. Limit them to only the essential points.
The problem of reducing the scope of tasks an agent can perform
Grant read-only permissions for the agent's identity, and invoke it using the user's identity, restricting actions to those the user is authorized to perform.
Even with guardrails, improper permission settings can result in broad scope. Check together with policies from external systems.
A method of enforcing a predefined limit per tool through code
Allow queries only to specific tables, verify arguments in pre-call and post-call callbacks
If tool modifications are difficult, callbacks can be used instead; however, policies that cannot be determined solely by arguments may not be filtered effectively.
data.notes: ADK explains two approaches: one where an agent accesses external systems using its own identity, and another where access is made using the identity of the current user. Both approaches follow the principle of overlapping with guardrails. Rather than relying on a single layer of protection, permissions and approvals are layered across the guardrails for input, tools, and output.

screens.outro: Since we've completed the categorization, I'll summarize the guardrail placement in one section.

screens.title: Arrange guardrail placement on one sheet.
screens.lead: Summarizes the previous content by organizing it according to the position of inspection, execution method, criteria, and relationship with other devices.

paragraphs: Input validation filters dangerous requests before processing, preventing costs and side effects. Tool validation checks arguments and results before and after calls that could cause side effects. Output validation prevents policy violations and sensitive information from being exposed to users before delivery. The three points do not substitute for one another.

The execution mode of input guardrails involves a trade-off between cost and latency. Use a costly model or block the agent from starting if the tool may cause side effects; otherwise, use parallel execution when side effects are absent but latency is more critical. Output guardrails execute after the agent completes, so this choice does not apply.

Balance is between oversight and overreaction. Being more strict does not make systems safer; instead, it increases the cost of normal operations being disrupted. Adjustments are made by recording inspection results, observing them, and tailoring them to match the nature of the service.

Finally, guardrails are not a panacea. Automated checks can be delegated to guardrails, but human approval is required when irreversible side effects are involved, and authority and separation of concerns should be applied when reducing the scope.

Going back to the initial question, the structure is that homework solutions are handled in the input phase, personal data leaks are prevented in the output and tool phases, and then permissions and approvals are layered on top. The core of this course is not asking agents to "don't do it," but rather implementing code-based checks before and after execution.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Guardrails are placed before and after execution. Input is validated before processing, tools are checked before and after invocation, output is validated before response is sent, and authorization limits and human approval are applied concurrently.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Apply guardrails to a customer support agent that has a costly model and order cancellation tools. Which execution approach is appropriate?
options: Parallel execution: Has the shortest delay and is acceptable for tools to run before tripwire.
Block execution: the agent starts only after the guardrail has finished.
Turn on the parallel option in the output guardrail to perform joint validation before responding.
Turn off the guardrail and only instruct the system prompt to not do so.
checks.explain: Blocking execution is appropriate when the cost is high or the tool may cause side effects. When Tripwire is enabled, the agent does not run, thereby preventing token consumption and side effects.

wrong.0: Parallel execution allows agents to use tokens and execute tools before tripwire is enabled.
wrong.2: Output guardrails run after the agent has completed, so there are no parallel options.
wrong.3: A prompt alone is insufficient; it requires code-based checks before and after execution.

checks.intro: Pair terms and explanations. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Pair the following terms and descriptions.
right: Filters out violations even with low confidence
Only filters when highly confident that a violation exists
Error allowing violation to pass through
Error determined as a violation of normal request
checks.explain: A panic is an error that blocks a normal request, while a trap is an error that allows a violation to pass. When the threshold is raised or lowered, the two swap roles.

checks.intro: This is a problem regarding judging a batch. No results are recorded.
checks.q: Before irreversible side effects occur, besides guardrails, what other mechanisms should be implemented?
options: The prompt instructs the model to use a longer instruction to encourage it to be more cautious.
Lowers the inspection threshold as low as possible to block all requests
Set a point to halt execution by human approval.
checks.explain: Actions that can be automatically evaluated are handled by guardrails, while actions with side effects—such as cancellation, editing, or transmission—are paused and require human approval. Permissions and isolation are applied together.

wrong.0: It is not enforced solely by instructions.
wrong.1: It becomes impossible to handle due to a significant increase in false positives that block even legitimate requests.
wrong.2: You should not rely on a single layer for protection; instead, permissions and approvals must be layered together.

glossary.def: A check placed on the user's initial input. It runs only at the first agent in the chain and filters out dangerous requests before they are processed.
A final check placed on the agent's output. It runs after the agent completes its task and prevents policy violations and sensitive information before being presented to the user.
This is the deviation switch included in the guardrail inspection results. If turned on, an exception occurs and execution is halted.

This is a mode where the guardrail starts simultaneously with the agent. While this approach has the minimum delay, when the tripwire is activated, the agent might have already used a token and executed a tool.
This is an error determined as violating a normal request. The occurrence increases as the inspection criteria become more stringent.

misconceptions.fact: Sensitive information or policy violations may occur in model outputs. Since responses do not exist during the input stage, separate output validation is required.

misconceptions.myth: Guardrails are automatically enabled across all agents and tools.
misconceptions.fact: Input is executed only by the first agent, and output is generated only by the agent that produces the final output. In workflows with extensive delegation, separate verification is required beside each tool.

misconceptions.myth: The stricter the inspection criteria, the safer it becomes.
misconceptions.fact: The more stringent the threshold, the more normal requests are blocked, leading to an increase in false alarms. The threshold balances between false alarms and missed detections, so it should be adjusted based on observed results.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Guardrails are placed before and after execution. Input is checked before processing, output is checked before response is sent, and tools are validated before and after invocation.
If the cost or side effects are high, perform blocking execution; if delay is critical, perform parallel execution.
Thresholds balance between oversight and negligence, and are adjusted by observing the results.
Guardrails are applied together with permission restrictions and human approvals.
